questions.title: Why use TypeScript in a large application?
questions.quick: TypeScript earns its place in a large codebase mainly through the compiler. Types describe the contracts between modules, so when a function signature or a data shape changes, every call site that no longer fits is flagged before the code ships. That makes refactoring far safer across many teams. Editors also get accurate autocomplete and navigation, which helps new engineers find their way around. The limits matter too. Types are erased at runtime, so they do not validate data coming from APIs or users, and they do not replace security controls or tests. I would pair TypeScript with strict mode and runtime validation at the boundaries.
questions.revision: Compiler-checked contracts make large-scale change safer; types vanish at runtime, so validate external data separately.
questions.detailed:
TypeScript adds a static type system on top of JavaScript. In a large application its main value is that the compiler checks how the parts of the codebase fit together before the code runs. Types document the contracts between modules, so a change to a function signature or a data shape produces errors at every affected call site instead of a runtime failure in production.

## Where it helps

- **Safer refactoring:** renaming a property or changing a parameter type shows every affected location in the editor and in CI.
- **Explicit contracts:** interfaces and type aliases describe what a module accepts and returns, which helps engineers read code without tracing every caller.
- **Better tooling:** autocomplete, go-to-definition and automated code changes rely on accurate type information.
- **Early detection:** misspelled property names, missing arguments and many null-handling mistakes are caught during compilation.

## What it does not do

Types are erased when the code is compiled to JavaScript. They describe the program as written, but they cannot check a JSON response from the network, a database row or an environment variable. Those values need runtime validation at the boundary. TypeScript also does not replace authorisation, input sanitisation or security review. Its guarantees depend on configuration: with loose settings and heavy use of `any`, many of the benefits disappear.

## Common mistakes

Teams sometimes assume a type annotation proves that data is valid, or they use `as` casts to silence the compiler. For example, an API response typed as `User` without any check lets a missing field fail deep inside business logic. A better pattern is to parse the response with a schema at the edge and let the rest of the code rely on the parsed type.

In practice, I would enable strict mode, keep public module interfaces explicit, validate external data, and treat the type system as one layer of quality alongside tests and code review.
